newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian wine industry sees premium vintage.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian wine industry sees premium vintage.

text.p: The Australian wine industry's intake of premium grape varieties in the 1997 vintage is expected to rise by up to 10 percent on 1996's bumper crop, driven by new plantings and surging exports of premium wine.
The Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) expects wine producers to crush 516,000 tonnes of premium varieties in 1997, up from last year's 477,000 tonnes.
While exact industry figures differ, the Winemakers Federation of Australia says there is agreement on the extent of the rise, as wine producers pursue the premium export market.
With the vintage due to begin in the New South Wales' Hunter Valley this weekend, leading companies are expecting their total crushes to approach or exceed last year's record levels.

Apart from spring frosts causing significant losses to sultanas and some loss to premium varieties like chardonnay in the Riverland and Sunraysia regions, producers say the vintage, which will extend through to April, is looking promising.

Philip Jaffer, chief winemaker at Australia's third largest winemaker Orlando Wyndham, owned by the French Pernod Ricard group, said overall the 1997 crop, in terms of yields per hectare, is lower than in 1996's bumper harvest.
"But the total crop of quality fruit will nevertheless be probably up, simply because of the new areas (of planting) coming into production," he told Reuters.
"From almost every point of view, it looks like being, right at this moment, an excellent vintage," he said.
While Australia's biggest wine producer, Southcorp Holdings Ltd, does not disclose its targets, sources said it expected to come close to last year's 180,000 tonne intake.

BRL Hardy Ltd said its intake was likely to be comparable to last year's 147,500 tonnes, with a big mix change towards more premium varieties, as with Orlando which is looking at crushing 105,000 tonnes, up on last year's 95,000 tonnes.

Mildara Blass, taken over last year by the Foster's Brewing Group, is looking to take in 45,000 tonnes, boosting last year's 35,000 tonnes through new plantings and acquisitions including its takeover of premium producer Rothbury Wines.
Bulk producer Simeon Wines Ltd is also aiming to meet last year's 56,000 tonnes, although it says it may struggle to do so and is currently advertising for more fruit.

The Winemakers' Federation of Australia anticipates a total 1997 vintage intake of at least 825,000 tonnes, significantly down from last year's 885,000 tonnes, but says the figure may be revised upwards as the vintage gets underway across all regions.
It says most of any reduction on last year's record vintage is expected to come through significantly fewer tonnages of the sultana variety, the mainstay of domestic bulk wine.
Federation chief executive Ian Sutton said 170,000 tonnes of sultanas were taken by producers in 1996, to build up dangerously low stocks from the disastrous 1995 vintage.
Angus Kennedy, operations and technical manager at BRL Hardy said there would be a shift of about 15,000 tonnes toward premium varieties in the company's expected crush this year.
Jaffer said Orlando's premium intake also would be up quite substantially, with premium varieties taking a 70 percent share of total intake compared to last year's 60 percent share.
The Winemakers' Federation said latest figures showed about 21,000 hectares of new vineyards had been planted in the past five years, a capital investment of more than A$600 million.
"This is clearly the year when supply and demand and pricing should all come into better balance, although we are going to be short of premium reds for the next few years," Sutton said.

The figure this year could drop by as much as 100,000 tonnes, due to lesser demand, lower yields and frost, he said. Southcorp's business development manager, Bruce McDougall, said the frost had also affected some premium varieties, including chardonnay, which would impact on prices.

"Before this frost we were expecting some significant downward pressure on varietal white prices (but we are expecting) only moderate pressure now," he told Reuters, adding that prices for reds would remain firm. -- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
